paras: The lynching of Henry Liste was the killing of a Black farmer by a band of whitecappers at his home in the Gum Grove neighborhood of Lincoln County, Mississippi, on the night of November 24, 1903. The riders had fired into his house and ordered him to leave about two weeks earlier, and they returned when he stayed. Newspapers treated the killing as evidence that whitecapping in the county, thought to have been suppressed, had revived in a worse form.

In mid-November 1903 a New Orleans dispatch reported that whitecaps were again ordering residents away in the McCall Creek neighborhood of Lincoln, Franklin and Amite counties, and that a state senator had laid complaints before Gov. Longino. The same dispatch said it had become almost impossible to secure Black laborers in the area. According to the Brookhaven Leader, whitecappers on the Saturday night before Liste's death riddled the house of Eli Hilson, a Black man living about seven miles from Brookhaven who had been warned to leave, though no one was hit.

Liste had lived in the community nearly all his life and, as far as the Leader could learn, bore a good reputation. He farmed a small place of his own, which the Leader said he had bought about a year earlier from A. C. Seavey & Sons of Brookhaven and on which he still owed money. About two weeks before his death whitecappers shot into his house and warned him to leave, but he decided to stay.

On the night of November 24 the whitecappers returned to Liste's house and, in the Leader's words, "literally riddled List and his house with bullets." He lived only a short while after the shooting. A New Orleans wire report described the attackers as "a large body of armed Whitecaps on horseback" who visited Black residents who had refused orders to leave the county. None of the reports gives any accusation against Liste beyond his refusal to go.

The wire report said public sentiment in the county was strongly against the whitecappers and that Gov. Longino had promised to take action. No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution for Liste's death appears in the coverage. In early December the Leader warned that the driving off of labor by whitecaps meant "enormous loss" to Lincoln County's farmers and businesses.

Eli Hilson was shot dead in his buggy near his home on December 19, and the Leader called him "the second negro murdered by whitecaps in that portion of Lincoln county within the last month." The Baltimore Afro-American, repeating that count, added that Black residents were "greatly alarmed" and deserting the county. In February 1904 the Atlanta Independent described Black laborers leaving Franklin, Amite and parts of Lincoln counties because of whitecapping.

The Brookhaven Leader broke the story on November 28 under the headline "MORE WHITE CAPPING IN LINCOLN," stressing Liste's good reputation and warning that whitecapping was "assuming a graver and more aggravated form." Two days later the New York Sun printed a New Orleans dispatch headed "WHITECAPS' TERRORISM" and "Negroes Persecuted," which spelled the name Lisle, placed him at "Green Grove," and called him "a negro farmer of excellent reputation." In early December several Mississippi weeklies, including the Brandon News, the Port Gibson Reveille and the Greene County Herald, ran a rewritten Brookhaven dispatch under the headline "'NIGHT RIDERS' RIOT AGAIN." The Brandon News also reduced the episode to a single line in its news digest.

Later coverage in the Leader framed whitecapping mainly as a threat to farm labor, land values and credit, while also calling for the "dastardly white cap outrages" to be suppressed. No Black newspaper in the coverage named Liste; the Baltimore Afro-American referred to his death only as an earlier, unnamed whitecap murder in its report on Hilson's killing.

The Leader dated the attack to "Thursday night (Nov. 24)," while the rewritten dispatch said Tuesday night; November 24, 1903 fell on a Tuesday. The local paper placed Liste in the Gum Grove neighborhood, whereas the New Orleans wire gave Green Grove. The Leader said Liste still owed money on his farm, but the rewritten dispatch said he had paid for it.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Liste
bases: A band of whitecappers who had earlier warned Henry Liste to leave and fired into his house returned at night and shot him to death in his home (A2, A3); the killing was part of a whitecapping campaign against Black residents of southwestern Lincoln County (A1, A3).

Liste was shot by night riders and died soon after (A2, A5); the New Orleans wire describes a 'large body of armed Whitecaps on horseback' visiting Black residents who refused orders to leave the county (A3), a racially targeted campaign of expulsion carried out outside the law (A1, A3).

The local Brookhaven Leader (A2) and a separate New Orleans wire dispatch with details the Leader lacks (A3) agree on the killing, the earlier warning and shooting, and the whitecappers' responsibility; the Brandon News version (A5) is a rewrite of the Brookhaven report rather than an independent source.

accounts.label: Brookhaven Leader (local)
accounts.gist: Whitecappers riddled Liste and his house with bullets on the night of Nov. 24, two weeks after they had shot into it and warned him to leave; he lived only a little while.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire
accounts.gist: A large armed band of Whitecaps on horseback killed Henry Lisle at Green Grove on their second visit; public sentiment was against them and the governor promised action.

accounts.label: Rewritten Brookhaven dispatch
accounts.gist: Same account as the Leader, but dated to Tuesday night, with the name Lisle and the farm described as paid for.

framing.detail: The Brookhaven Leader headlined 'MORE WHITE CAPPING IN LINCOLN,' described Liste as of good reputation, and warned that whitecapping was 'assuming a graver and more aggravated form.'
The New York Sun ran the wire under 'WHITECAPS' TERRORISM' and 'Negroes Persecuted,' calling Lisle 'a negro farmer of excellent reputation.'
Mississippi weeklies ran the Brookhaven story under '"NIGHT RIDERS" RIOT AGAIN' alongside unrelated items on a truck crop and a near collision, and one digest reduced it to a single line.
After Hilson's murder the Leader framed whitecapping as an economic threat to farmers and lenders and called for the 'dastardly white cap outrages' to be suppressed.

The Baltimore Afro-American, under 'MURDERED BY WHITE CAPS,' mentioned the earlier killing only as an unnamed second murder and stressed Black flight from the county; the Atlanta Independent later described the exodus of Black laborers from the whitecapped counties.

conflicts.note: November 24, 1903 fell on a Tuesday, and the Leader's 'last Saturday' attack on Hilson would be Nov. 21, so the date Nov. 24 and the Tuesday agree; the Leader's 'Thursday' is likely an error.
The local Brookhaven paper, and the version derived from it, give Gum Grove; the distant wire gives Green Grove. The local report is the better evidence.
Spelling varies; the local paper uses both Liste and List in one article.
